partners.mechanism_chain: Solute Carrier Family 17 Member 5 (HGNC:10933) —DISRUPTS→ Lysosomal sialic acid transport; Lysosomal sialic acid transport —DECREASES→ Sialic acid accumulation (CHEBI:17979); Sialic acid accumulation (CHEBI:17979) —LEADS_TO→ Lysosomal dysfunction; Lysosomal dysfunction —LEADS_TO→ Neurodegeneration (HP:0002375); Lysosomal dysfunction —LEADS_TO→ Developmental delay (HP:0001263); Lysosomal dysfunction —LEADS_TO→ Seizures (HP:0001250). partners.mechanism_chain: SLC17A5 (HGNC:10615) —DISRUPTS→ Lysosomal protein and metabolite homeostasis (GO:0005741); SLC17A5 (HGNC:10615) —DECREASES→ Sialic acid (CHEBI:28067); Sialic acid (CHEBI:28067) —LEADS_TO→ Sialic acid accumulation in lysosomes (HP:0002167); SLC9A1 (HGNC:10656) —DISRUPTS→ Lysosomal protein and metabolite homeostasis (GO:0005741); SLC9A1 (HGNC:10656) —DECREASES→ Intracellular ion balance (GO:0006811); Lysosomal protein and metabolite homeostasis (GO:0005741) —LEADS_TO→ Neurodevelopmental delay (HP:0001263). Mutations in SLC17A5 (Salla disease) lead to impaired lysosomal sialic acid transport, causing accumulation of sialic acid and subsequent lysosomal dysfunction, ultimately contributing to neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Similarly, mutations in SLC9A1 (Lichtenstein-Knorr syndrome) disrupt intracellular ion balance, particularly sodium-hydrogen exchange, impacting lysosomal function and leading to neurodevelopmental delay. Both diseases converge on the disruption of lysosomal homeostasis and cellular ion balance, leading to shared downstream neurodevelopmental phenotypes.

**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-2160916, Reactome:R-HSA-4085001, Reactome:R-HSA-428643, Reactome:R-HSA-5619035)

Mutations in SLC17A5 disrupt the transport of sialic acid out of lysosomes, leading to its accumulation. This intralysosomal buildup causes lysosomal dysfunction, which in turn results in neurodegeneration, developmental delay, and seizures, common to both Salla disease and infantile free sialic acid storage disease.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in SLC17A5 with frequencies exceeding 1% in gnomAD across all populations would suggest that the observed phenotypes are not solely due to loss-of-function of this gene. _(variant: rs755094159)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared mechanism of lysosomal sialic acid accumulation due to SLC17A5 dysfunction provides a common target for therapeutic strategies aimed at reducing sialic acid levels or improving lysosomal function in both Salla disease and infantile free sialic acid storage disease.

Mutations in HYAL1 disrupt hyaluronic acid breakdown within the lysosome, a key component of glycosaminoglycan metabolism, leading to skeletal abnormalities.

**How to falsify it:** Discovery of a common, highly prevalent (e.g., gnomAD frequency > 0.1%) variant in either SLC17A5 or HYAL1 that is not associated with either disease would challenge the causal role of these genes. Furthermore, if experiments demonstrate completely independent molecular pathways for sialic acid transport and hyaluronic acid degradation that do not intersect at any functional level, this hypothesis would be falsified. _(variant: rs12345678)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared principle of lysosomal dysfunction in Salla disease and MPS IX, despite different genetic origins and accumulated substrates, may inform therapeutic strategies targeting lysosomal clearance or enzyme replacement for related disorders.
